chapter_theme: Paripadal 7, to the Vaiyai: the rain-fed flood coming down from the hills to the Pandya fields, the town's cries and the river's spoils likened to the king's conquest, the lovers' quarrels of the water-play, and a closing prayer never to leave the river.

paripadal:7:1-22.reading: Clouds that have drawn up the cold dark sea break open like a tank whose bank has given way, with thunder roaring, and white falls wind round every hill like the risen ranks of the Pandya's army marching day and night on its chosen land; so the Vaiyai's water comes, swelling the land's good and its beauty, scattering narantham and vengai flowers, uprooting wind-bent trees and spreading their fruit over the low ground; while the ploughmen revel and the drums sound, it goes where it will like a girl who knows no dance and a joyful one who knows no sulking, fighting every dam, and like a paste mixed by rule it hides the common smells within and gives off a new fragrance, this red-flowered flood.
paripadal:7:1-22.nuance: The flood is carried by the cycle that begins at sea (line 1) and ends in the fields' good (line 9, நலன் நந்த நாடு அணி நந்த), so the praise of the river is also praise of rain. The two similes of lines 17 and 18 already give the river a woman's temper, a girl untaught and without oodal, which the water-play later in the song turns round: there the women quarrel and the river stays calm.

thinai_evidence.note: description and praise of the river's coming, in a song addressed to Vaiyai: paadaan

paripadal:7:23-50.reading: On every side the town cries out: the flood has spread over the lilies of the pond, it has wrecked the dolls the young women drew in the sand and they weep, it has reached the cut sheaves of young paddy so the drum is beaten, the tide has ringed the town, the sky has lost its sluices; it has taken the singers' hamlet and the dancers' street, run into the fields, let the carp eat the spathes, raised the seed-beds into mounds; it rushes like the swell of desire, the field-workers with the shoaling carp spread the water, the banks are guarded like hills, it bears hill-like foam, roofs itself with flowers and spreads through the groves; and as the bathers deck their ears and pluck their garlands, it carries off bangles, rings, armlets, cloth and girdles, entering like the Pandya into the land of his enemies: such is the beauty of the Vaiyai of the king whose army killed his foes.
paripadal:7:23-50.nuance: The list of cries (lines 23 to 35) is the flood seen by those it harms, and the poet keeps it in praise: losses of sand dolls and seed-beds are counted as the river's wealth. The closing simile turns the river's taking of the bathers' jewels into the Pandya's plunder of enemy country, so the river's beauty (வனப்பு, line 50) is put in the king's possession. Lines 36 and 37 (the swell of desire that joins women who will not understand when told) are hard to construe; the flood's speed seems compared to the haste of passion.

thinai_evidence.note: the river's flood and its spoils told as praise of the Pandya's Vaiyai: paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the flood seizing the bathers' ornaments

paripadal:7:51-76.reading: Among the bathers the water is flung till flower-like eyes redden; one woman, unashamed and proud, takes a man captive in her soft shoulders, and a gold-creeper of a girl leaps to free him from her grip, and the light of their kohl eyes, like a keen iron blade, darkens the red new flood; another, to dry her wet ornaments, lifts bee-humming toddy, and her neythal eyes turn to the strong drink; then a bard, seeing a woman's eyes, sings many songs in praise of her watery glance, and one woman, hating the song, is overcome, the broad-chested lover trembles at what will come to him, and she, eyes red with oodal, quarrels among the women, tears her garland, and in a fury brings down her man, who had looked at the ornaments of the bathing bodies, into the mud and treads on his head, fighting without end while the whole town bathes in the red flood.
paripadal:7:51-76.nuance: The song moves from the river's beauty to a lovers' quarrel without leaving the flood: the oodal of lines 67 to 76 is caused by the bard's praise of another woman's eyes and by the man's looking (யாறு ஆடு மேனி அணி கண்ட, line 73), and it is told as a public scene, the town going on with its bathing around it. The trembling lover (என்னை வருவது எனக்கு?, line 68) is comic, and the head trodden in the mud is the akam sulk acted out in full. No colophon names a speaker; the poet narrates, so there is no thurai_akam.

thinai_evidence.note: a jealous sulk at a river bathing, the marutham situation of oodal

comparisons.tenor: the girl who rushes to free the man
the eyes of the woman holding toddy

paripadal:7:77-86.reading: The seven paalai modes on the twisted strings, the lute and the voice join, the flute keeps the measure, the drum rises and roars, and the women of the king's house and the singers begin to dance; the beauty of the water that pours down fighting its banks is like the roar where thunder strikes; and the poet hails the Vaiyai of the bewildering water, whose bathers at the ford of Tirumarutham wear garlands on their heads: singing your bounty till dawn we are safe, and pray that we may bathe in you and never leave it, now that we have joined.
paripadal:7:77-86.nuance: The music of lines 77 to 80 is the festival's, and the poem's own pan is பாலையாழ், so the song names its mode inside itself (பாலை ஏழும், line 77). Line 85 has a gap; the closing prayer asks for the bathing never to end (நீங்காமை, line 86), the same wish akam lovers make of each other, here made of the river.

thinai_evidence.note: the closing address and prayer to the river: paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the roar of the water pouring down

links.note: Kural 17 says even the wide sea would lose its nature if the cloud that drew from it gave nothing back; Paripadal 7.1-10 begins with clouds that have drawn the dark sea fully (பௌவம் செவ்விதா அற முகந்து) and ends the sentence with the land's good and beauty swelling as the Vaiyai comes.
links.teaches: The couplet states the exchange between sea and cloud as a warning about withholding, while the song follows the same water through rain, falls and river into the Pandya fields, so together they show that the Kural's abstract cycle was the felt shape of the flood festival, praised in the hymn as the return the couplet only demands.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 69 has the wife say she has seen the husband's woman crying, eyes reddened, when the cool flood with its flowers swept her sand-play away at the crowded ford; Paripadal 7.25-26 lists among the town's cries the young women weeping that the flood broke the dolls they drew in the sand.
links.teaches: In the hymn the weeping over sand dolls is one anonymous cry among many on flood day, while the akam wife picks out one such girl to mock as her husband's new woman, so the pair shows the akam poet taking a stock festival scene and turning it into a mark of the rival's childishness.

links.note: Akananuru 266 has the wife tell her husband that his bathing yesterday in the new flood with young women, gazing again and again at one woman's rain-cool eyes, is now loud gossip; Paripadal 7.65-76 shows the scene itself: a bard praises a bather's eyes, the lover who looked at the bathers is pulled into the mud and his head trodden on by the woman in her sulk.
links.teaches: The Akananuru gives only the aftermath, the wife's reproach once talk has spread, whereas the Paripadal shows the gazing at the eyes and the quarrel breaking out at once in the river, so together they show the river bathing as the very occasion of the marutham sulk, with its offence and its punishment both public.

links.note: Kural 1311 has the woman refuse her lover's chest because all women feast on him with their eyes; in Paripadal 7.69-75 the woman's fury falls on her lover because he looked at the ornaments of the bathing women (யாறு ஆடு மேனி அணி கண்ட).
links.teaches: The couplet makes the man's being looked at enough for oodal, the hymn makes his looking the offence, and the song's crowded bathing shows why both could be true at once: in the festival everyone sees and is seen, so the sulk needs no act of straying, only the eyes.

links.note: Naladiyar 370 makes the fresh flood (புதுப்புனல்) a type of what does not last: it ends when the rain ends; Paripadal 7.84-86 prays to the Vaiyai's flood that the bathing in it may never be left (நின் படிந்து நீங்காமை).
links.teaches: The same new flood that the ethical quatrain uses to prove that pleasures and loves dry up is, in the festival hymn, the object of a prayer for permanence, so the pair shows the didactic poet reversing the devotional value of the river by fixing on its ending rather than its yearly return.

source_issues: Paripadal 7: the colophon has no thinai or thurai; only the subject வையை, the poet மையோடக் கோவனார், the music and the pan பாலையாழ் (a musical mode, not a thinai) are given.
Paripadal 7 line 85 has a gap (lacuna); the close of the prayer is incomplete.
Paripadal 7 lines 11 and 12 are not in sangamtamil.com's text; line 38 had ொ restored and line 81 was replaced by the sangamtamil.com reading (flags).
Paripadal 7 line 15: உய்ர்ந்துழி reads as a misprint for உயர்ந்துழி.
Paripadal 7 lines 36-37 and 54-57 are hard to construe: who is captured and who frees whom is not certain.
